svg.aria-label: Diagram: what enabling Workload Identity Federation for GKE creates, the credential flow from application default credentials through the GKE metadata server and Security Token Service, the four principal identifiers and the namespace one that spans clusters, and the two cases where a Pod authenticates as the node instead
svg.title: Workload Identity for GKE: Google manages the provider, and the pool belongs to the project
svg.text: No external provider, no attribute mapping, no condition to forget.
Google Cloud manages the pool and provider for you. The risk reappears as a naming question instead.
Enabling it creates three things
A fixed pool: PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog
— note the scope in the name: PROJECT.
The cluster registered as a provider in it.
The GKE metadata server, intercepting
credential requests, on every node.
The credential flow
1. ADC asks the Compute Engine metadata server.
2. GKE metadata server intercepts, asks the
Kubernetes API server for a KSA token (a JWT).
3. STS exchanges it for a short-lived token.
The trust ends at the API server’s signature.
Four identifiers — and one is wider than it reads
/subject/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/SERVICEACCOUNT
all Pods using that ServiceAccount
/kubernetes.serviceaccount.uid/UID
the same, tied to that exact object
/namespace/NAMESPACE
ALL Pods in that namespace — ANY cluster
/kubernetes.cluster/...
all Pods in ONE named cluster
The catch: the namespace identifier crosses clusters, because the pool is the PROJECT
One pool per project, every cluster registered inside it. So a grant to /namespace/prod does not mean
“the prod namespace in this cluster”. It means prod ANYWHERE in the project — the staging cluster that
also has one, the cluster created next quarter, the cluster restored during an incident.
Namespace names are meant to repeat across clusters. That is exactly what makes this dangerous.
And the pool outlives the clusters: deleting every cluster leaves it, and your grants, in place.
Two ways a Pod authenticates as something else
hostNetwork: true — does NOT use federation at all.
Routed to the Compute Engine metadata server, so it authenticates as the NODE. Nothing warns.
The first few seconds — the metadata server is not ready yet.
An intermittent cold-start auth failure that gets misdiagnosed as a flaky grant. Retry, do not re-grant.
Enabling grants nothing: it creates identities, and the allow policies are still yours to write.
The node service account still pulls images — empty it and you get ImagePullBackOff, which looks nothing like IAM.
Capacity ceiling: 6,000 token exchanges per minute. High Pod churn reaches it, and it presents as an identity fault.
The recurring shape of this block: the better the convention, the wider the grant that follows it.
